title: The Skeleton That Rebuilds Itself
blurb: The 206 bones inside you are alive, and they tear themselves down and build themselves back up your whole life.

blocks.prompt: The Skeleton That Rebuilds Itself
blocks.text: Feel the top of your head. Knock on it gently. That hard round part is your skull. It is a helmet made of bone, and it keeps your brain safe. Now feel your chest. Those bumpy lines are your ribs. They make a cage around your heart and lungs. Bones are not soft, but they are alive. They grow while you grow. When you were a baby, you had about 300 bones. Some of them joined together as you got bigger. Grown-ups have 206.

your heart and lungs

3.title: The Skeleton That Rebuilds Itself
3.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 7 to 8

blocks.prompt: The Frame You Are Wearing
blocks.text: Your skeleton has three jobs, and it does all of them at once. The first job is holding you up. Without bones you would fold onto the floor like a coat with no hanger. The second job is armor. Your skull is a hard case around your brain. Your ribs curve around your heart and lungs like the bars of a cage. The third job is moving. Bones cannot move by themselves. Muscles pull on them, and the bones swing at the joints, the places where two bones meet. Here is the part people forget. Bones are alive. Blood runs through them. Inside the big ones is a soft middle called marrow, and marrow makes new blood for you every second of the day. Your longest bone is in your thigh. It is called the femur. Your smallest bone is deep inside your ear, and it is about the size of a grain of rice. Your hands and feet are packed with small bones. Together they hold more than half of all the bones in your body.

answers: holding you up, armor, and moving
a place where two bones meet
it makes new blood every second
(inference: a hard case protects the brain from bumps)

4.title: The Skeleton That Rebuilds Itself
4.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 9 to 10
4.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Some questions ask what you think, not just what the passage says.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Living bone is warm and slightly bendy
Collagen bends, minerals resist crushing
Osteoclasts remove bone, osteoblasts build it
Your skeleton is replaced about every 10 years
Astronauts lose bone because nothing loads it

blocks.prompt: The Skeleton That Rebuilds Itself
blocks.text: Picture a bone and you probably picture something dry and dead, the kind of thing hanging in a science classroom. A living bone is nothing like that. It is warm. It is slightly flexible. It is threaded with blood vessels and nerves, which is exactly why a broken one hurts so much. A bone is built from two materials working together. Collagen, a stretchy protein, gives it the ability to bend a little instead of shattering. Hard minerals, mostly calcium, give it the strength to carry your weight. Rope alone would be too floppy. Chalk alone would snap. Bone is both at once, which is why, ounce for ounce, it can take more squeezing force than steel can. Stranger still, your skeleton never sits still. Two kinds of cells work on it every day of your life. Osteoclasts crawl along the bone and dissolve small patches of it away. Osteoblasts follow behind and lay down fresh bone in the gaps. The demolition crew and the construction crew work the same site, forever. Little by little, the old material is swapped out for new. Most of your skeleton is replaced roughly every ten years. The bones you have now are not the bones you had in kindergarten, even though they have kept the same shape the whole time. This constant rebuilding lets bone respond to what you ask of it. Load a bone by running, jumping, or lifting, and the building crew thickens it where the force lands. Stop loading it, and the crew stops bothering. Astronauts learn this the hard way. In orbit, where nothing weighs anything, their bones lose mass month after month, so they strap themselves to machines and exercise for hours a day just to keep the skeleton they arrived with.

5.title: The Skeleton That Rebuilds Itself
5.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 11 to 12
5.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Use evidence from the text where the question asks for it.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Long bones are hollow tubes, not solid rods
Inside the ends is a lattice of fine struts
The struts line up with the paths force takes
Wolff's law: bone adapts to the load it carries
A tennis player's serving arm is denser
Broken bone rebuilds, it does not scar

blocks.prompt: Built by the Load
blocks.text: Saw a thigh bone in half and you find it is not solid. The outer wall is dense and compact, but the interior is a lattice of thin struts and open spaces, like the inside of a sponge frozen in place. This looks like a weakness. It is the opposite. Solid bone that thick would be far too heavy to carry around, and the open design gives nearly the same strength for a fraction of the mass. Engineers copied the idea for bridges and aircraft long after bone had settled on it. Look closer at those struts and the design gets sharper. They are not scattered at random. They run along the exact lines that force travels through the bone. In the head of the femur, where your body weight turns a corner to enter your leg, the struts fan out in curving arcs that trace the path of the load. A nineteenth century anatomist named Julius Wolff noticed that these arcs matched the stress diagrams engineers drew for loaded structures. The rule that carries his name says that bone adapts to the forces placed on it: bone that is worked gets stronger, and bone that is left idle gets thinner. That rule only works because bone is alive and under constant renovation. Osteoclasts dissolve old material and osteoblasts rebuild it. Where a bone is loaded, the rebuilding crew outpaces the demolition crew and the structure thickens. Where a bone is idle, the balance tips the other way. A tennis player's serving arm carries visibly denser bone than the other arm. An astronaut in orbit, weightless and therefore unloaded, sheds bone mass at roughly one percent a month, faster than most people lose it in a year on the ground. The same living quality explains something you may take for granted. When you cut your skin, it heals with scar tissue, a patch that seals the gap but never restores what was there. Bone does not settle for that. A break is bridged first by a soft collar of cartilage, then hardened into bone, then slowly reshaped over months until the repair matches the original architecture, struts and all. A well healed bone is not patched. It is rebuilt. So the skeleton is not the frame you were issued at birth and have been carrying ever since. It is a structure that reads the forces you put through it and quietly redesigns itself to match.

6.title: The Skeleton That Rebuilds Itself
6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Bone is a composite: collagen plus calcium mineral
About a tenth of the skeleton is rebuilt each year
99 percent of body calcium is stored in bone and teeth
Marrow makes roughly 2 million red blood cells a second
Wolff's law: bone adapts to the loads it carries
The hyoid is the only bone joined to no other bone

blocks.prompt: The Skeleton Is Not a Frame
blocks.text: The skeleton in the corner of a science classroom is a lie, or at least a very poor translation. It is dry, still, and mineral, and it teaches you to think of your bones as scaffolding: inert poles that hold the interesting parts in place. Almost every part of that impression is wrong. Bone is a living tissue, richly supplied with blood and nerves, rebuilt continuously from the day you are born, and it is doing at least three jobs at once, two of which have nothing to do with holding you up. Start with the material. Bone is a composite, which means it is two substances that fail in different ways, combined so that neither failure happens. The first is collagen, a protein laid down in fibers, tough and slightly elastic. The second is a calcium mineral packed into and around those fibers, rigid and enormously resistant to being crushed. Collagen alone would be rope. Mineral alone would be chalk. Together they produce a material that resists both bending and crushing at a weight your muscles can actually move, and engineers have spent decades trying to imitate the arrangement. Then look at the architecture, because the shape is as clever as the substance. The shaft of a long bone is a hollow tube, and a hollow tube resists bending almost as well as a solid rod of the same width at a fraction of the weight. Inside the ends, where forces arrive from odd angles, bone abandons the tube and builds a lattice of fine struts aligned along the paths that stress actually takes. The nineteenth century anatomist Julius Wolff noted that this pattern matched the stress trajectories engineers calculated for loaded structures, and the principle now named after him holds that bone adapts to the loads it carries. A tennis player's serving arm is measurably denser than the other. An astronaut, unloaded in orbit, loses bone at around one percent a month. That responsiveness is possible only because the skeleton is under permanent renovation. Osteoclasts dissolve old bone and osteoblasts deposit new. Roughly a tenth of your skeleton is torn down and rebuilt each year, so that over about a decade the structure is quietly replaced without ever once ceasing to work. This is where the second job hides. Your nerves fire and your heart beats only if the calcium concentration in your blood stays inside a narrow band, and about ninety nine percent of your body's calcium is locked in your bones and teeth. When blood calcium falls, hormones instruct the osteoclasts to open the vault. Your skeleton is not only a structure. It is a bank, and the bank will be robbed to keep the chemistry alive, because a body with slightly weaker bones survives, and a body with the wrong blood calcium does not. The third job runs in the hollow you have already been introduced to. Inside your larger bones sits marrow, and marrow is a factory producing red blood cells at a rate of roughly two million per second, every second, for your whole life. The organ that holds you upright is also the organ that stocks your blood. Hold all three jobs together and the skeleton stops looking like a frame. It is a load bearing structure, a chemical reserve, and a blood factory, built from the same material, competing for the same material, and constantly renegotiating the settlement between them. You are not carrying your skeleton around. It is carrying you, and it is arguing with itself the entire time.
